title: Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL)
summary: Defines the Simple Authentication and Security Layer, a framework for authentication and data security in connection-oriented protocols through replaceable mechanisms. It lets new protocols reuse existing mechanisms and old protocols adopt new ones. It obsoletes RFC 2222 and is standards-track.

eli5.summary: Different apps need to check who you are. SASL is a standard plug socket so any app can use any login method.

questions: what is the sasl external mechanism
what is a sasl security layer
subtitle: A plug-in framework that lets any connection-oriented protocol use any authentication mechanism, with an optional protection layer.

tldr.problem: Each protocol that needed login would otherwise have to design its own authentication, and adopting a new method would mean redesigning the protocol.
tldr.mechanism: SASL defines an abstraction layer: a protocol supplies messages to start an exchange, carry challenges and responses, and report the outcome, while replaceable mechanisms define what is inside. A negotiated security layer can then protect later traffic.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2222, tightens requirements on protocols and mechanisms, and defines one mechanism, EXTERNAL.

today: RFC 4422 is a Proposed Standard and the status metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 2222, whose KERBEROS_IV and SKEY mechanisms are now Historic.

sections.title: A Framework Between Protocols and Mechanisms
sections.content:
The Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) is a framework for authentication and data security in connection-oriented protocols via replaceable mechanisms. It gives protocols and mechanisms a structured interface, and it also defines how to secure later protocol exchanges in a data security layer that can provide integrity, confidentiality and other services.

The RFC draws SASL as an abstraction layer. Protocols such as SMTP, LDAP and XMPP sit above it, and mechanisms such as EXTERNAL, GSSAPI and PLAIN sit below. The layer does not hide everything: mechanisms still need different inputs, such as passwords, realms, Kerberos tickets or certificates.

The document serves three audiences: protocol designers, mechanism designers, and implementors of clients and servers.
sections.eli5: Think of a wall socket. Any lamp can plug in, and the power company can change how it makes electricity without changing the lamps.

sections.title: Authentication and Authorization Identities
sections.content:
SASL involves two identities. The authentication identity goes with the credentials, such as a certificate or a username and password. The authorization identity is the identity to act as. The client may send a string naming the authorization identity; if it is omitted or empty, the client asks to act as the identity tied to its credentials.

The server checks two things: that the credentials are valid, and that the identity tied to them may act as the requested identity. The exchange fails if either check fails. Mechanisms define the credential and authentication identity forms, while protocols define the form of the authorization identity. How identities of different forms relate is otherwise a local matter.
sections.eli5: Showing your library card proves who you are. Asking to borrow a book for your little brother is a second question: are you allowed to act for him?

sections.title: The Authentication Exchange
sections.content:
An exchange has the client request authentication with a named mechanism, then one or more pairs of server challenges and client responses, then the server's outcome. Either side may abort. Mechanism names are 1 to 20 characters of uppercase ASCII letters, digits, hyphens and underscores.

Round trips can be saved. If the mechanism lets the client speak first and the protocol has an initial response field, the client sends it with the request. Otherwise the server sends an empty challenge. Likewise, if a mechanism has the server send additional data with success and the protocol has a field for it, it travels in the outcome message. If not, it goes as a challenge answered by an empty response. A client that sends an initial response for a mechanism that does not allow client-first fails the exchange.

Mechanism negotiation is protocol specific and is not protected by the exchange, so it is open to downgrade attacks unless protected by other means. The outcome is unsuccessful if, for example, credentials cannot be verified, the requested authorization identity is not allowed, or the negotiated security layer is unsuitable. Unless the protocol says otherwise, only one successful exchange may occur in a session.
sections.eli5: It is a polite conversation: the client says which kind of password game to play, the server asks questions, the client answers, and then the server says yes or no.

sections.title: The Security Layer
sections.content:
If a security layer is negotiated, the server installs it after sending the outcome and the client installs it on receiving the outcome, both before further protocol data. It stays in effect until another layer replaces it or the connection closes. If the outcome is unsuccessful, or no layer was negotiated, any existing security is left in place.

Protected data is sent in buffers, each prefixed by a four-octet length field in network byte order. The buffer MUST be no larger than the maximum size the other side expects, and a receiver that sees a larger length SHOULD close the connection, since that may be an attack. If the layer cannot produce or decode protected data, the connection MUST be closed. Only one security layer may be in effect at a time.
sections.eli5: After the login, the two sides can put every message in a locked, sealed box. Each box has its size written on the outside so nobody can sneak in a giant one.

sections.title: What Protocols and Mechanisms Must Specify
sections.content:
A protocol that offers SASL MUST supply: a service name taken from the GSSAPI host-based service name registry, its mechanism negotiation facility, the messages to start an exchange, carry challenges and responses, and give the outcome, the syntax of non-empty authorization identity strings, how exchanges can be aborted, where a new security layer takes effect, the order of layers if others such as TLS exist, and whether multiple authentications are supported. The protocol SHOULD let the client discover the mechanism list both before the exchange and after the security layer is installed, so that downgrades can be detected. Protocols SHOULD be mechanism neutral.

A mechanism specification MUST give its registered name, its challenges and responses, whether it is client-first, variable or server-first, whether it sends additional data on success, whether it can carry an authorization identity, and whether it offers a security layer. New mechanisms SHOULD carry authorization identity strings, SHOULD use UTF-8, and SHOULD specify SASLprep for simple user names and passwords. Mechanisms SHOULD NOT use the authorization identity string for long-term cryptographic keys or hashes.
sections.eli5: Both the app and the login method must write down their side of the deal in detail, so that any app and any login method fit together without surprises.

sections.title: Attacks and Defences
sections.content:
The RFC says many existing mechanisms give inadequate protection against passive attacks, let alone active ones, and many offer no security layer. It notes that the SASL framework itself is susceptible to downgrade attacks.

An active attacker can alter the mechanism list or the mechanism name sent in the clear. Defences include not advertising or accepting mechanisms that fail one's minimum requirements, and having the client fetch the mechanism list again after an integrity-protecting layer is installed. If that list holds a stronger mechanism than the first one, the client should assume tampering and SHOULD close the connection. Replay may affect some mechanisms unless external services such as TLS protect them. Most existing layers do not stop truncation attacks. A receiver MUST NOT blindly allocate memory for the length in a buffer header.

The SASL framework does not itself provide re-keying, though mechanisms may. Passive attacks include eavesdropping on unprotected credentials and dictionary attacks.
sections.eli5: A sneaky person in the middle might trick both sides into using the weakest lock. The fix is to check again, once the sealed box is working, that the strong locks really were on offer.

sections.title: The Mechanism Registry
sections.content:
IANA keeps a SASL mechanism registry. Individual mechanism names are registered First Come First Served with no review of the claims made, while a family name (a prefix such as X-) needs expert review. Each registration says whether usage is COMMON, LIMITED USE or OBSOLETE. Registrations cannot be deleted, only marked OBSOLETE.

This document updated the registry so that KERBEROS_V4 and SKEY are marked OBSOLETE and EXTERNAL points to RFC 4422 as its specification.
sections.eli5: There is a public name list of login methods. Anyone can add a name, and old methods get a sticker that says OBSOLETE rather than being erased.

sections.title: The EXTERNAL Mechanism
sections.content:
Appendix A defines EXTERNAL. It lets the client ask the server to use credentials set up by means outside the mechanism, such as IP Security or TLS. The client cannot assume which external means the server used. There is no security layer. The client sends first, with the UTF-8 form of the requested authorization identity, or an empty response to act as the identity tied to its credentials. There are no further challenges, and the server returns the outcome without additional data.

The exchange fails if the client has no credentials by external means, the credentials are inadequate, the authorization identity is invalid or not allowed, or the server is otherwise unable to serve. EXTERNAL gives no protection itself and should only be used when adequate security has been established.
sections.eli5: EXTERNAL says: I already showed my ID at the front gate, so please just trust that.

messages.note: Any negotiated security layer is installed after this.
